newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - New supply to weigh on market.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - New supply to weigh on market.

text.p: UK gilts may gain ground against vulnerable U.S. Treasuries this week but they will have a tough time matching Bunds' performance, as new supply and the looming election weigh on the UK market, analysts said on Monday.
After last week's sharp rally at the short end, investors are unlikely to find much value in the short sterling strip, they added.
"I really can't see gilts pushing too far ahead this week with the new supply coming through," said Union Plc economist Philip Uglow.
The market will have to absorb 4.0 billion sterling of new stock this week.
The Bank of England is due to auction 2.5 billion stg of 7.25 percent gilts maturing in 2007 on Tuesday, followed by 1.5 billion stg of 7.0 percent gilts maturing in 2002 on Thursday.
"The auctions should be the main influence on the gilt curve," said Societe Generale analyst Brian Hilliard.
"We expect the supply pressure to hurt the 10-year sector but not the five year as the latter will be the last such issue for the fiscal year."
Huw Roberts from NatWest Markets said the new 10-year stock should be well received by the market due to its strippable status and small issue size.
This, and the long dated stock auction due on February 26, should ensure that the 10-20s spread will widen, Roberts said.
Analysts said the new supply meant gilts would probably underperform Bunds this week.
"We think most of the good news is already priced into the market and that sterling will make little headway during the week ahead," said Hilliard.
"With the dual auction and the general election looming, we recommend playing the widening of the gilt/Bund spread again towards 190 basis points."

On Monday morning, the 10-year gilt/Bund spread was at 183 basis points. "That's fairly near the bottom of the recent range so I don't think people will be looking at that and saying that it's particularly good value," said Union's Uglow.
Key data from the U.S. this week could upset nervous Treasuries and bring gilts down in their wake, analysts said.

The fourth quarter employment cost index, due on Tuesday, will give a guide to U.S. inflation which, combined with Q4 GDP data on Friday, will set the tone for the Federal Open Market Committee meeting in early February.

"If we see the ECI ticking up substantially from the 2.8 percent last time, there will be fears of increasing wage pressures and people will be looking to the February 4-5 meeting as a possible time the Fed might tighten," said Uglow.
"If we do see stronger data in the States...that may lead to a global selling of bonds."
Societe Generale's Hilliard said short sterling may suffer some profit-taking this week after its recent rally.
"Short sterling, which has rallied almost to excessive levels, now implying base rates by the year end below seven percent, is likely to give up some more ground to profit taking," he said.
Other domestic data this week include trade figures on Tuesday and December consumer credit data on Thursday.
"The consumer credit data should be market supportive as we expect a softer figure than seen in recent months," said Hilliard.
According to a Reuter survey, economists expect consumer credit to rise by 928 million stg in December, following November's 1.105 billion stg increase.
